tagline: A remote East Gippsland coast of empty beaches, dunes and lighthouses
description: Croajingolong is a linear coastal national park in East Gippsland, about 80 km long and 20 km wide, with the Tasman Sea to the south and Mallacoota at its eastern end. Rocky outcrops, long sandy beaches, coastal dunes and freshwater rivers suit hiking, swimming, snorkelling and sea kayaking. The Wilderness Coast Walk follows the shore, and Point Hicks is believed to be Captain Cook's first Australian landfall. UNESCO nominated the park a World Biosphere Reserve in 1977, and it holds almost 1,000 native plant species.
whyVisit: Walk a wild coast of empty beaches
Paddle coastal inlets and rivers
Stay in historic lighthouse cottages

goodToKnow.title: Bring your own food
goodToKnow.detail: Outside Mallacoota there is nowhere to eat or buy supplies in the park, so stock up in town before heading in.

goodToKnow.title: Unsealed roads need 4WD
goodToKnow.detail: Mallacoota is the only town and the park has no other paved roads. Reaching places like Point Hicks needs a good 4WD.

bestTimeBlurb: Warm {months} days suit beach walks, paddling and camping on this exposed coast.
notes: No source states best months; derived from climate. Parks Victoria page returned no content. Wilderness Coast Walk permit tip left out (rank 4 gets two tips).

tagline: A gold-rush city of grand Victorian buildings, mines and Chinese heritage
description: Gold found on Bendigo Creek in 1851 turned a sheep station into one of colonial Australia's largest boomtowns, drawing migrants from Europe and China. The wealth built grand Victorian public buildings, and Sacred Heart Cathedral is the third-largest cathedral in Australia. Visitors can go underground at Central Deborah Gold Mine and see Sun Loong, the world's longest imperial dragon, at the Golden Dragon Museum. Bendigo is Victoria's fourth-largest city, about 140 km north-north-west of Melbourne.
whyVisit: Go underground in a gold-rush mine
Admire grand Victorian architecture
See art at a major regional gallery

goodToKnow.title: Book for Easter
goodToKnow.detail: The Easter Festival procession draws tens of thousands over the long weekend, so book beds well ahead.

goodToKnow.title: Summer gets hot
goodToKnow.detail: Days above 35 C are common in summer and the record is 45.4 C. Plan mine and walking visits for morning.

goodToKnow.title: Ride the talking tram
goodToKnow.detail: The tourist tram links the Central Deborah mine and the Chinese heritage sites, so it works as a loop tour.

bestTimeBlurb: Mild {months} days suit mine tours and walks, while summer often tops 35 C.
notes: Easter Festival is a yearly pattern; no seasonalTags written since tag format is not in the brief. Gallery reason is general (no named exhibition).

tagline: Gateway to the Grampians with gold-rush, Chinese and asylum history
description: Ararat is about 200 km north-west of Melbourne on the Western Highway and is known as the Gateway to the Grampians. Gold found in 1857 made it a boomtown, and it is the only city in Australia founded by Chinese people, a story told at the Gum San Chinese Heritage Centre. Visitors can tour J Ward, the former home of the criminally insane, and the Aradale asylum. Seppelt at Great Western, a short drive away, has 3 km of 1800s tunnels, the largest underground cellar in the Southern Hemisphere.
whyVisit: Tour the old asylum buildings
Taste wine at nearby cellar doors

goodToKnow.title: Train from Melbourne
goodToKnow.detail: V/Line runs trains from Southern Cross several times daily, and The Overland to Adelaide stops twice a week.

goodToKnow.title: Book cellar tours
goodToKnow.detail: Seppelt's tunnel tours run at set times, listed as 11am, 1pm and 3pm, for a fee, so check times before driving out.

bestTimeBlurb: Mild {months} weather suits touring wineries and heritage sites.
notes: Best months derived from climate (warm summers with cold fronts, cool rainy winters), not a recommendation from a source. Tunnel tour times should be re-checked.

tagline: A Port Phillip peninsula of seaside towns, beaches and coastal wineries
description: The Bellarine Peninsula lies south-west of Melbourne between Port Phillip, Corio Bay and Bass Strait. It became a holiday destination in the 1870s, when Melbourne visitors came by paddle steamer to fish and swim, and is now known for beaches, seaside resorts, small towns and wineries. The Bellarine Railway runs tourist services between Drysdale and Queenscliff, with a rail trail alongside. Burrunan dolphins and Australian fur seals are among the marine life seen around the coast.
whyVisit: Stroll historic seaside streets
Swim and surf at beach towns
Taste wine at coastal vineyards

goodToKnow.title: Cross by ferry
goodToKnow.detail: The Queenscliff to Sorrento ferry takes cars to the Mornington Peninsula and saves driving round the bay.

goodToKnow.title: Summer crowds
goodToKnow.detail: The population roughly doubles in peak summer, so book stays early and arrive at beaches before midday.

bestTimeBlurb: Beach season peaks {months} and crowds double the population, so aim for the quieter end.
notes: Wikivoyage redirects to Greater Geelong. Summer-only seasonal tag is unverified so omitted.

tagline: South-west Victoria's largest town, with shipwreck history and a volcano reserve
description: Warrnambool is the largest town in south-west Victoria, about 260 km west of Melbourne, and is sometimes treated as the end of the Great Ocean Road. Flagstaff Hill Maritime Museum has a replica maritime village and a night show telling the story of the Loch Ard wreck. Tower Hill, 14 km west, is an extinct volcano that erupted at least 34,000 years ago and is now a wildlife reserve. A 37 km rail trail links the town with Port Fairy via Koroit.
whyVisit: Watch southern right whales from shore
Learn shipwreck history at a maritime village
Walk the rim of an extinct volcano

goodToKnow.title: Whale season June-September
goodToKnow.detail: Southern right whales visit Logans Beach from June to September. Check the visitor centre for confirmed sightings.

goodToKnow.title: Allow time to drive
goodToKnow.detail: Melbourne is about 3.5 hours by the Princes Highway and longer along the Great Ocean Road, so plan an overnight.

bestTimeBlurb: Southern right whales visit Logans Beach {months}, often close enough to see without binoculars.
notes: Whale season is a yearly pattern; no seasonalTags written since tag format is not in the brief. 'Walk the rim' follows the research experience list.

tagline: A high-country gateway to Mount Buller skiing, lakes and mountain trails
description: Mansfield is a country town about two hours' drive north-east of Melbourne and the support town for Mount Buller ski resort. Mount Buller has 22 lifts, the highest lift capacity in Victoria, while Mount Stirling is a cross-country and backcountry ski area. In summer, hiking and mountain biking are popular on both mountains, and Lake Eildon is the only inland waterway in Victoria where houseboats are permitted. Mansfield is also on the Ned Kelly Trail.
whyVisit: Ski and snowboard in winter
Hike and bike the high country
Houseboat and waterski on big lakes

goodToKnow.title: Carry wheel chains
goodToKnow.detail: Wheel chains must be carried on the road up to Mount Buller throughout the winter season.

goodToKnow.title: Drive up from Melbourne
goodToKnow.detail: Mansfield is reached by car, about two hours via the Yarra Valley. Allow extra time on winter weekends.

bestTimeBlurb: Winter snow and summer lakes and trails make {months} the best times to visit.
notes: Exact ski season dates not sourced. Ski season could be a seasonal tag but dates unverified, so omitted.

tagline: A bay-and-ocean peninsula south of Melbourne with hot springs and vineyards
description: The Mornington Peninsula lies south of Melbourne on the eastern side of Port Phillip Bay, about 40 km long and tapering to Point Nepean. The bay side has sheltered sandy beaches for families, while the ocean side is popular with surfers. Peninsula Hot Springs has mineral-rich thermal pools up to 50 C, and Arthurs Seat reaches 305 m with wide views from its summit road. Point Nepean has an old fort and quarantine station, and is where Prime Minister Harold Holt vanished while swimming in 1967.
whyVisit: Soak in thermal hot springs
Walk coastal cliffs and bay beaches
Taste wine at cellar doors

goodToKnow.title: Drive or ferry in
goodToKnow.detail: Public transport is limited beyond the main towns, so a car helps. The Sorrento-Queenscliff car ferry runs hourly, 7am-6pm.

goodToKnow.title: Pack a jacket in winter
goodToKnow.detail: Summer is busiest, but cold-season storms on the Bass Strait beaches are dramatic. Bring a jacket.

goodToKnow.title: Hot springs peak pricing
goodToKnow.detail: Peninsula Hot Springs charges peak-time prices and has had age limits, so check both before going with young children.

bestTimeBlurb: The peninsula is at its best and busiest in {months}, with sheltered bay beaches and surf.
notes: Hot springs under-5 rule was from an older guide, so the tip is worded to check. Ferry hours should be re-checked.

tagline: Fern gullies, hill villages and a heritage steam railway east of Melbourne
description: The Dandenong Ranges are low mountain ranges about 35 km east of Melbourne, rising to 633 m at Mount Dandenong, topped by a TV tower. Puffing Billy, a heritage steam railway, runs 24 km on its original mountain track from Belgrave to Gembrook and is the most popular attraction in the ranges. Sheltered gullies hold temperate rainforest, tree ferns and mountain ash forest, with superb lyrebirds and kookaburras. The ranges have been a day-trip and weekend retreat for Melburnians since the 1870s.
whyVisit: Ride a steam train through the hills
Walk fern gullies and tall forest
Wander quiet hill villages

goodToKnow.title: Train from Melbourne
goodToKnow.detail: Belgrave line trains reach Belgrave in just over an hour, where Puffing Billy departs. Buses up the hills run rarely.

goodToKnow.title: Dress for the hills
goodToKnow.detail: Daytime temperatures run 4 to 6 C cooler than Melbourne's lower suburbs, and winter fog is common.

goodToKnow.title: Check fire restrictions
goodToKnow.detail: The ranges are bushfire-prone and summer fire restrictions apply. There is no camping in the national park and no rubbish bins.

bestTimeBlurb: Cooler, milder {months} weather suits walking, before summer fire restrictions and winter fog.
notes: Autumn colour and spring garden timing not sourced, so not claimed.
